title: Getting Control of Your Life: The Five Stages of Mastering Workflow
coreMove: Run every piece of stuff through capture, clarify, organize, review, and engage before trusting your choices.

exampleSpecs.domain: a hospital charge nurse clearing end-of-shift scraps from pockets and handoff notes
exampleSpecs.audience: a nurse responsible for keeping patient follow-ups from disappearing between shifts
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a family callback, medication question, or supply request gets lost because it stayed as a half-memory
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the nurse captures every loose reminder into one visible inbox before deciding importance, showing that collection comes before judgment

exampleSpecs.domain: a public defender leaving a crowded arraignment calendar with vague case notes
exampleSpecs.audience: a lawyer carrying many live obligations with court deadlines attached
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a client’s next filing stalls because 'handle Rivera matter' is not yet a defined outcome or action
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the lawyer turns a vague note into the desired outcome and one next physical action instead of rereading it as if concern were progress

exampleSpecs.domain: a high school band director preparing for a spring concert while fielding permission slips, instrument repairs, and parent emails
exampleSpecs.audience: a teacher who has many small commitments arriving through many channels
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether concert logistics become a noisy pile or a set of reminders that can be found when needed
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director sorts clarified items into calendar, next-action, waiting-for, and reference places rather than keeping one mixed master list

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional warehouse supervisor doing a Friday review before next week's inventory audit
exampleSpecs.audience: an operations lead whose work depends on seeing the whole map before Monday starts
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether missing vendor confirmations and staffing gaps surface early enough to fix
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the supervisor reviews projects, waiting-fors, calendars, and action lists until the system feels current enough to stop mentally reheating the audit

exampleSpecs.domain: a traveling medical-device repair technician stuck in an airport delay with a phone, thirty minutes, and low energy
exampleSpecs.audience: a field technician who must choose useful work from changing conditions
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the delay becomes anxious scrolling or a realistic choice among calls, forms, and parts requests
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the technician chooses from context, time, energy, and priority instead of from whichever reminder shouts loudest

exampleSpecs.domain: a restaurant line cook newly promoted to shift lead after a chaotic weekend service
exampleSpecs.audience: a first-time supervisor learning why busyness alone does not create control
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether repeated shortages, schedule questions, and prep mistakes keep recurring because no stage of workflow is being completed
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the shift lead traces the breakdown to skipped capture, unclear next actions, and unreviewed waiting-fors rather than blaming people for not trying hard enough

exampleSpecs.domain: a small-town building inspector talking with a homeowner after a storm-damage visit
exampleSpecs.audience: a municipal worker balancing public service, forms, field visits, and callbacks
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a resident gets a clear repair-permit path or another vague promise to 'look into it'
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the inspector names what the item is, what done would look like, where the reminder will live, and the very next contact to make
